On ARMOR this produced `bf-3b64` (\"Starvation alert: beads invisible to worker\") at 2026-07-06T12:45:30Z. A dispatched worker did the standard investigate→fix→verify→monitor decomposition on it — reasonable-looking, except the \"fix\" step (`bf-36co`, \"Fix bead discovery configuration\") asks a worker scoped to the *target* repo to edit **NEEDLE's own** filter/exclude_labels configuration, which is not part of that repo and is not reachable or editable from inside it. The fix bead stayed permanently blocked.\n12\t\n13\tBecause the alert never actually resolved, later sessions kept re-triggering it and re-investigating from scratch — near-duplicate \"Locate Pluck configuration files\" beads were independently recreated at least 3 times. One investigative thread guessed the unreachable config was YAML-formatted and pivoted from \"find the config\" to \"build a YAML parser to read it,\" which — lacking any real target file to validate against — snowballed into open-ended, self-justifying busywork: a full YAML/JSON/TOML parser library, then a pytest-output-parsing tool, then hundreds of near-duplicate test-coverage beads (folded-scalar indentation matrices, schema interfaces, scope-stack tracking), continuously, for 8 days. Total damage on ARMOR alone: 346 fabricated beads, ~2,300 combined bead-cycles across two workers, while 5 real, actually-dispatched beads sat untouched the entire time. A parallel instance of the same pattern was found mid-execution on `~/SIGIL` (worker `echo`), not yet cleaned up.\n14\t\n15\t**Bug 2 — fleet process tracking has blind spots.** Remediating the above required stopping the runaway workers, which surfaced a second, independent defect:\n16\t- `needle stop -i <session>` reported success and removed the session from `needle list`, but the underlying OS process (the actual `needle run --workspace ...` process and its dispatched `claude` subprocess) kept running and kept dispatching against the target repo. It had to be killed directly by PID (`kill -9`) after cross-referencing `ps aux`.\n17\t- A third worker (`alpha`, also pointed at ARMOR, also actively dispatching) was running the entire time and was **completely invisible to both `needle status` and `needle list`** — discovered only via `ps aux | grep 'needle run'`.\n18\t\n19\tBoth bugs share a root theme: NEEDLE's own operational state (what it's confused about, what it's running) leaks into or is undiscoverable from the wrong place — the target repo's bead tracker in Bug 1, nowhere-queryable in Bug 2.\n20\t\n21\t## Decision\n22\t\n23\t1. **Redirect Pluck's starvation self-diagnostic to NEEDLE's own telemetry.** Never write it as a bead into the scanned workspace. Emit a structured `pluck.starvation_detected` telemetry event (workspace, open count, excluded count, candidate reasons) through the existing telemetry pipeline (the same one `ExploreStrand`'s Phase-5 starvation alarm uses — see ADR-001 §5.4). If a persistent, actionable record is wanted, file it as a bead in **NEEDLE's own** workspace, never the target's.\n24\t2. **Treat \"Pluck configuration is unreachable from a target-scoped worker\" as a structural constraint, not a solvable task.** A target-repo worker must never be prompted to investigate or fix NEEDLE's own dispatch configuration — that class of work has no legitimate resolution path from inside the target repo and should be filtered out of what gets auto-decomposed there.\n25\t3. **`needle stop` must kill the full process tree**, not just detach/remove the tmux registry entry: parent `needle run` process, its `bash -c` prompt wrapper, and the dispatched `claude` subprocess. Verify the PID is actually gone before reporting success, not just that the tmux session no longer lists it.\n26\t4. **`needle status`/`needle list` must not have registry blind spots.** Every `needle run` process, however it was started (tmux-wrapped, bare `NEEDLE_INNER=1` background, etc.), must be discoverable through standard fleet commands. Reconcile the process-table view (`ps aux`) against the registry view as a health check, and WARN on any process matching `needle run --workspace` that isn't in the registry.\n27\t\n28\t## Consequences\n29\t\n30\t- Pluck's starvation signal becomes debuggable (NEEDLE operator telemetry) instead of destructively actionable (a bead a worker will try, and fail, to resolve).\n31\t- Removes the specific self-perpetuating loop that produced this incident; does not by itself prevent all forms of worker rabbit-holing (that's the broader failure-circuit-breaker problem tracked elsewhere).\n32\t- `needle stop` becomes trustworthy for incident response — an operator (or Claude, acting on an operator's behalf) can rely on \"Stopped: X\" actually meaning the process is gone, without a manual `ps aux` cross-check.\n33\t- Slightly more telemetry volume (one starvation event per strand-scan-with-nothing-claimable); bounded the same way ADR-001's starvation alarm is.\n34\t- `~/SIGIL`'s parallel instance of Bug 1 is not fixed by this ADR alone — it needs its own cleanup pass once this fix ships, the same way ARMOR did.\n35\t\n36\t## Evidence\n37\t\n38\t- `~/ARMOR` bead `bf-3b64` (created 2026-07-06T12:45:30Z) and its full descendant lineage — 346 beads total, closed 2026-07-14 across three review passes.\n39\t- Lab fleet state 2026-07-14: `bravo` (1671 beads) and `echo` (566 beads) on ARMOR/SIGIL respectively, both >99% consumed by beads matching this lineage; `ps aux` showed PID 143883 (`needle run --workspace /home/coding/ARMOR --identifier alpha`), running since 2026-07-11, still dispatching against the same duplicated bead (`bf-4tshoo`) as `bravo`.\n42\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"e1311c42-de3b-4d60-bd06-829751ff36c3","uuid":"46cf3225-da71-4725-b942-752b2fed935e","timestamp":"2026-07-15T14:03:37.406Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/home/coding/NEEDLE/docs/adr/002-pluck-telemetry-isolation-and-process-tracking.md","content":"# ADR-002: Pluck Telemetry Isolation and Fleet Process Tracking\n\n**Status:** Accepted — 2026-07-14\n**Deciders:** operator (jedarden)\n**Tracking:** plan.md Phase 6; A dispatched worker did the standard investigate→fix→verify→monitor decomposition on it — reasonable-looking, except the \"fix\" step (`bf-36co`, \"Fix bead discovery configuration\") asks a worker scoped to the *target* repo to edit **NEEDLE's own** filter/exclude_labels configuration, which is not part of that repo and is not reachable or editable from inside it. The fix bead stayed permanently blocked.\n\nBecause the alert never actually resolved, later sessions kept re-triggering it and re-investigating from scratch — near-duplicate \"Locate Pluck configuration files\" beads were independently recreated at least 3 times. One investigative thread guessed the unreachable config was YAML-formatted and pivoted from \"find the config\" to \"build a YAML parser to read it,\" which — lacking any real target file to validate against — snowballed into open-ended, self-justifying busywork: a full YAML/JSON/TOML parser library, then a pytest-output-parsing tool, then hundreds of near-duplicate test-coverage beads (folded-scalar indentation matrices, schema interfaces, scope-stack tracking), continuously, for 8 days. Total damage on ARMOR alone: 346 fabricated beads, ~2,300 combined bead-cycles across two workers, while 5 real, actually-dispatched beads sat untouched the entire time. A parallel instance of the same pattern was found mid-execution on `~/SIGIL` (worker `echo`), not yet cleaned up.\n\n**Bug 2 — fleet process tracking has blind spots.** Remediating the above required stopping the runaway workers, which surfaced a second, independent defect:\n- `needle stop -i <session>` reported success and removed the session from `needle list`, but the underlying OS process (the actual `needle run --workspace ...` process and its dispatched `claude` subprocess) kept running and kept dispatching against the target repo. It had to be killed directly by PID (`kill -9`) after cross-referencing `ps aux`.\n- A third worker (`alpha`, also pointed at ARMOR, also actively dispatching) was running the entire time and was **completely invisible to both `needle status` and `needle list`** — discovered only via `ps aux | grep 'needle run'`.\n\nBoth bugs share a root theme: NEEDLE's own operational state (what it's confused about, what it's running) leaks into or is undiscoverable from the wrong place — the target repo's bead tracker in Bug 1, nowhere-queryable in Bug 2.\n\n## Decision\n\n1. **Redirect Pluck's starvation self-diagnostic to NEEDLE's own telemetry.** Never write it as a bead into the scanned workspace. Emit a structured `pluck.starvation_detected` telemetry event (workspace, open count, excluded count, candidate reasons) through the existing telemetry pipeline (the same one `ExploreStrand`'s Phase-5 starvation alarm uses — see ADR-001 §5.4). If a persistent, actionable record is wanted, file it as a bead in **NEEDLE's own** workspace, never the target's.\n2. **Treat \"Pluck configuration is unreachable from a target-scoped worker\" as a structural constraint, not a solvable task.** A target-repo worker must never be prompted to investigate or fix NEEDLE's own dispatch configuration — that class of work has no legitimate resolution path from inside the target repo and should be filtered out of what gets auto-decomposed there.\n3. **`needle stop` must kill the full process tree**, not just detach/remove the tmux registry entry: parent `needle run` process, its `bash -c` prompt wrapper, and the dispatched `claude` subprocess. Verify the PID is actually gone before reporting success, not just that the tmux session no longer lists it.\n4. **`needle status`/`needle list` must not have registry blind spots.** Every `needle run` process, however it was started (tmux-wrapped, bare `NEEDLE_INNER=1` background, etc.), must be discoverable through standard fleet commands. Reconcile the process-table view (`ps aux`) against the registry view as a health check, and WARN on any process matching `needle run --workspace` that isn't in the registry.\n\n## Consequences\n\n- Pluck's starvation signal becomes debuggable (NEEDLE operator telemetry) instead of destructively actionable (a bead a worker will try, and fail, to resolve).\n- Removes the specific self-perpetuating loop that produced this incident; does not by itself prevent all forms of worker rabbit-holing (that's the broader failure-circuit-breaker problem tracked elsewhere).\n- `needle stop` becomes trustworthy for incident response — an operator (or Claude, acting on an operator's behalf) can rely on \"Stopped: X\" actually meaning the process is gone, without a manual `ps aux` cross-check.\n- Slightly more telemetry volume (one starvation event per strand-scan-with-nothing-claimable); bounded the same way ADR-001's starvation alarm is.\n- `~/SIGIL`'s parallel instance of Bug 1 is not fixed by this ADR alone — it needs its own cleanup pass once this fix ships, the same way ARMOR did.\n\n## Evidence\n\n- `~/ARMOR` bead `bf-3b64` (created 2026-07-06T12:45:30Z) and its full descendant lineage — 346 beads total, closed 2026-07-14 across three review passes.\n- Lab fleet state 2026-07-14: `bravo` (1671 beads) and `echo` (566 beads) on ARMOR/SIGIL respectively, both >99% consumed by beads matching this lineage; the 5 real ARMOR Phase-5 integrity beads (genesis `bf-4l7q`) untouched throughout.\n- `needle stop -i needle-claude-code-glm-4_7-bravo` → \"Stopped\" → `ps aux` on the lab host still showed PID 144019 (`needle run --workspace /home/coding/ARMOR --identifier bravo`) alive and dispatching, 8+ minutes later.\n- `needle status`/`needle list` output on the lab host, checked repeatedly during remediation, never listed a worker named `alpha`; `ps aux` showed PID 143883 (`needle run --workspace /home/coding/ARMOR --identifier alpha`), running since 2026-07-11, still dispatching against the same duplicated bead (`bf-4tshoo`) as `bravo`.\n","numLines":42,"startLine":1,"totalLines":42}}}

Worker state registry — shared JSON file tracking all active workers.\n//!\n//! The registry is informational: \"who is running, what are they doing, how\n//! many beads processed.\" It is NOT used for coordination — heartbeats handle\n//! that.\n//!\n//! File: `~/.needle/state/workers.json`\n//! Access: flock-protected read-modify-write (atomic updates).\n//!\n//! Depends on: `config`, `types`.\n\nuse std::path::{Path, PathBuf};\n\nuse anyhow::{Context, Result};\nuse chrono::{DateTime, Utc};\nuse fs2::FileExt;\nuse serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};\n\n// ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n// PID liveness checking (platform-specific)\n// ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n\n/// Check if a process with the given PID is currently running.\n///\n/// Returns `false` if the PID does not exist or if we lack permission to signal it.\n/// This is best-effort: if we can't determine liveness, we assume the process is dead\n/// to avoid counting stale entries toward concurrency limits.\npub fn is_pid_alive(pid: u32) -> bool {\n    #[cfg(unix)]\n    {\n        // Use libc::kill with signal 0 to check if process exists.\n        // SAFETY: kill(pid, 0) only checks existence, doesn't send a signal.\n        unsafe {\n            let ret = libc::kill(pid as i32, 0);\n            if ret == 0 {\n                // kill succeeded: process exists and we have permission to signal it.\n                return true;\n            }\n            // kill failed: check errno to distinguish EPERM from ESRCH.\n            // We must read errno immediately after kill, before any other syscalls.\n            let errno = *libc::__errno_location();\n            match errno {\n                libc::ESRCH => {\n                    // No such process: PID is dead.\n                    false\n                }\n                libc::EPERM => {\n                    // Process exists but we don't have permission to signal it.\n                    // We treat this as \"alive\" since the process actually exists.\n                    true\n                }\n                _ => {\n                    // Other errors (e.g., EINVAL for invalid signal).\n                    // Conservatively treat as dead to avoid false positives.\n                    false\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n\n    #[cfg(not(unix))]\n    {\n        // On non-Unix platforms, conservatively return false (assume dead).\n        // This prevents false positives where dead PIDs are counted as live.\n        // TODO: Implement Windows liveness check via OpenProcess if needed.\n        false\n    }\n}\n\n// ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n// WorkerEntry\n// ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n\n/// A single worker entry in the registry.\n#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, PartialEq)]\npub struct WorkerEntry {\n    /// Fully-qualified worker identity (`{adapter}-{worker_id}`, e.g., `claude-foxtrot`).\n    pub id: String,\n    /// Process ID of the worker.\n    pub pid: u32,\n    /// Workspace the worker is processing beads from.\n    pub workspace: PathBuf,\n    /// Agent adapter name.\n    pub agent: String,\n    /// Model name (if known).\n    pub model: Option<String>,\n    /// Provider name (e.g., `anthropic`, `openai`).\n    pub provider: Option<String>,\n    /// When the worker started.\n    pub started_at: DateTime<Utc>,\n    /// Number of beads processed so far.\n    pub beads_processed: u64,\n}\n\n// ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n// RegistryFile\n// ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n\n/// The on-disk JSON structure for `workers.json`.\n#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]\npub struct RegistryFile {\n    pub workers: Vec<WorkerEntry>,\n    pub updated_at: DateTime<Utc>,\n}\n\nimpl Default for RegistryFile {\n    fn default() -> Self {\n        RegistryFile {\n            workers: Vec::new(),\n            updated_at: Utc::now(),\n        }\n    }\n}\n\n// ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n// Registry\n// ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n\n/// Worker state registry with flock-protected read-modify-write access.\n#[derive(Clone)]\npub struct Registry {\n    path: PathBuf,\n}\n\nimpl Registry {\n    /// Create a registry instance pointing at the given state directory.\n    ///\n    /// The directory will be created on first write if it does not exist.\n    pub fn new(state_dir: &Path) -> Self {\n        Registry {\n            path: state_dir.join(\"workers.json\"),\n        }\n    }\n\n    /// Create a registry using the default state directory (`~/.needle/state`).\n    pub fn default_location(needle_home: &Path) -> Self {\n        Self::new(&needle_home.join(\"state\"))\n    }\n\n    /// Path to the workers.json file.\n    pub fn path(&self) -> &Path {\n        &self.path\n    }\n\n    /// Register a worker on startup.\n    ///\n    /// If a worker with the same ID already exists, it is replaced (handles\n    /// stale entries from previous runs).\n    pub fn register(&self, entry: WorkerEntry) -> Result<()> {\n        self.modify(|reg| {\n            // Remove any existing entry with the same ID (stale from previous run).\n            reg.workers.retain(|w| w.id != entry.id);\n            reg.workers.push(entry);\n        })\n    }\n\n    /// Deregister a worker on shutdown.\n    ///\n    /// Best-effort: errors are logged but not propagated to avoid masking\n    /// the real shutdown reason.\n    pub fn deregister(&self, worker_id: &str) -> Result<()> {\n        self.modify(|reg| {\n            reg.workers.retain(|w| w.id != worker_id);\n        })\n    }\n\n    /// Update a worker's beads_processed count.\n    pub fn update_beads_processed(&self, worker_id: &str, beads_processed: u64) -> Result<()> {\n        self.modify(|reg| {\n            if let Some(entry) = reg.workers.iter_mut().find(|w| w.id == worker_id) {\n                entry.beads_processed = beads_processed;\n            }\n        })\n    }\n\n    /// Update a worker's current workspace.\n    pub fn update_workspace(&self, worker_id: &str, workspace: &Path) -> Result<()> {\n        self.modify(|reg| {\n            if let Some(entry) = reg.workers.iter_mut().find(|w| w.id == worker_id) {\n                entry.workspace = workspace.to_path_buf();\n            }\n        })\n    }\n\n    /// Read all registered workers, filtering out entries for dead PIDs.\n    ///\n    /// This lazy cleanup ensures that workers killed via SIGKILL or crashes\n    /// don't accumulate in the registry and falsely count toward concurrency\n    /// limits.\n    pub fn list(&self) -> Result<Vec<WorkerEntry>> {\n        let reg = self.read()?;\n        let total_count = reg.workers.len();\n        let live_workers: Vec<WorkerEntry> = reg\n            .workers\n            .into_iter()\n            .filter(|w| is_pid_alive(w.pid))\n            .collect();\n\n        // If we filtered out dead entries, persist the cleanup so we don't\n        // need to re-check their PIDs on every read. This is best-effort:\n        // if the write fails (disk full, race with another writer), we still\n        // return the correctly filtered list — we'll just re-filter next time.\n        let live_count = live_workers.len();\n        if live_count != total_count {\n            let dead_count = total_count - live_count;\n            tracing::debug!(dead_count, \"filtered dead worker entries from registry\");\n\n            let cleaned_reg = RegistryFile {\n                workers: live_workers.clone(),\n                updated_at: Utc::now(),\n            };\n            if let Err(e) = self.write_cleaned(cleaned_reg) {\n                tracing::warn!(\n                    error = %e,\n                    \"failed to persist dead PID cleanup; will re-filter next read\"\n                );\n            }\n        }\n\n        Ok(live_workers)\n    }\n\n    /// Write a cleaned registry file (used by list() to persist dead PID filtering).\n    ///\n    /// No file locking: read() already released its shared lock before returning.\n    /// The atomic rename ensures concurrent writers don't corrupt the file —\n    /// one write wins cleanly.\n    fn write_cleaned(&self, reg: RegistryFile) -> Result<()> {\n        let tmp_path = self.path.with_extension(\"json.tmp\");\n        let json = serde_json::to_string_pretty(&reg).context(\"failed to serialize registry\")?;\n        std::fs::write(&tmp_path, &json)\n            .with_context(|| format!(\"failed to write temp registry: {}\", tmp_path.display()))?;\n        std::fs::rename(&tmp_path, &self.path).with_context(|| {\n            format!(\"failed to rename temp registry to: {}\", self.path.display())\n        })?;\n        Ok(())\n    }\n\n    // ── Internal helpers ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n\n    /// Read the registry file, returning a default if it doesn't exist.\n    fn read(&self) -> Result<RegistryFile> {\n        if !self.path.exists() {\n            return Ok(RegistryFile::default());\n        }\n\n        let file = std::fs::File::open(&self.path)\n            .with_context(|| format!(\"failed to open registry: {}\", self.path.display()))?;\n\n        // Shared lock for reading (use fs2 trait method explicitly for MSRV compat).\n        FileExt::lock_shared(&file)\n            .with_context(|| format!(\"failed to acquire shared lock: {}\", self.path.display()))?;\n\n        let content = std::fs::read_to_string(&self.path)\n            .with_context(|| format!(\"failed to read registry: {}\", self.path.display()))?;\n\n        FileExt::unlock(&file)\n            .with_context(|| format!(\"failed to release lock: {}\", self.path.display()))?;\n\n        if content.trim().is_empty() {\n            return Ok(RegistryFile::default());\n        }\n\n        serde_json::from_str(&content)\n            .with_context(|| format!(\"failed to parse registry JSON: {}\", self.path.display()))\n    }\n\n    /// Perform a flock-protected read-modify-write operation.\n    fn modify<F>(&self, mutator: F) -> Result<()>\n    where\n        F: FnOnce(&mut RegistryFile),\n    {\n        // Ensure the parent directory exists.\n        if let Some(parent) = self.path.parent() {\n            std::fs::create_dir_all(parent).with_context(|| {\n                format!(\"failed to create registry directory: {}\", parent.display())\n            })?;\n        }\n\n        // Open or create the file.\n        let file = std::fs::OpenOptions::new()\n            .read(true)\n            .write(true)\n            .create(true)\n            .truncate(false)\n            .open(&self.path)\n            .with_context(|| format!(\"failed to open registry: {}\", self.path.display()))?;\n\n        // Exclusive lock for writing (use fs2 trait method explicitly for MSRV compat).\n        FileExt::lock_exclusive(&file).with_context(|| {\n            format!(\"failed to acquire exclusive lock: {}\", self.path.display())\n        })?;\n\n        // Read current contents.\n        let content = std::fs::read_to_string(&self.path).unwrap_or_default();\n        let mut reg: RegistryFile = if content.trim().is_empty() {\n            RegistryFile::default()\n        } else {\n            serde_json::from_str(&content).unwrap_or_default()\n        };\n\n        // Apply the mutation.\n        mutator(&mut reg);\n        reg.updated_at = Utc::now();\n\n        // Write back atomically: write to temp file, then rename.\n        let tmp_path = self.path.with_extension(\"json.tmp\");\n        let json = serde_json::to_string_pretty(&reg).context(\"failed to serialize registry\")?;\n        std::fs::write(&tmp_path, &json)\n            .with_context(|| format!(\"failed to write temp registry: {}\", tmp_path.display()))?;\n        std::fs::rename(&tmp_path, &self.path).with_context(|| {\n            format!(\"failed to rename temp registry to: {}\", self.path.display())\n        })?;\n\n        // Release lock (use fs2 trait method explicitly for MSRV compat).\n        FileExt::unlock(&file)\n            .with_context(|| format!(\"failed to release lock: {}\", self.path.display()))?;\n\n        Ok(())\n    }\n}\n\n//
